analysis.one_liner: Ends free gold and copper mining on public land, charging royalties and fees to clean up abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to two House committees on July 10, 2014, sent to subcommittees within a week, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1872 mining law, companies can take gold, silver, copper, and other hardrock minerals from federal land without paying the government any share of the value, and land can be bought (patented) for very little. This bill would put an 8% royalty on production, block most new patents, charge annual claim fees, close some sensitive lands to new claims, require mining companies to post bonds covering full cleanup costs, and channel the money into a fund to reclaim old abandoned mines. It also encourages volunteer cleanups of abandoned mine sites with limited legal protection for the volunteers.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and communities near mines. Today the public gets nothing when companies extract gold and other minerals from federal land, and taxpayers foot much of the bill for cleaning up abandoned mines that leak acid and heavy metals into water. The bill would collect an 8% royalty, annual fees, and a per-ton reclamation fee, deposit them in a dedicated fund, and require cleanup bonds so companies—not the public—pay to restore mined land and water. It would also let states, local governments, and tribes petition to protect watersheds and sacred places from new mining claims.

how_it_helps.text: Production of locatable minerals would be subject to an 8% royalty on gross income, with a reduced 4% rate for mines already operating, and no royalty at all for small producers with under $100,000 in annual mineral income.
Mining companies would have to post financial assurance covering the full cost of reclamation and water treatment before starting work, and restore mined land to support prior or beneficial uses.

Operators would pay a 7-cents-per-ton fee on displaced material, plus annual claim maintenance fees, into a Hardrock Minerals Fund dedicated to reclaiming abandoned mine lands and assisting affected communities.

States, local governments, and Indian tribes could petition to withdraw specific federal lands from mining to protect drinking water, wildlife, or cultural and sacred sites, and sensitive areas such as wilderness study areas and roadless areas would be closed to new claims.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, who would pay an 8% royalty for the first time, annual claim fees, a per-ton reclamation fee, and the full cost of bonding and cleanup. Small miners with under $100,000 in income or fewer than 10 claims are exempted.

drawbacks.text: The 8% royalty, per-ton fee, and full-cost bonding would raise production costs for mining companies, which industry argues could discourage domestic mineral production and cost jobs in mining towns; the bill's small-producer exemptions soften but do not eliminate this cost.

The new permitting system, with exploration and operations permits, financial assurance, and public participation requirements, would add time and expense before projects could begin, a real cost even for projects that end up approved.

The Good Samaritan provisions shield volunteer cleanups of abandoned mines from Clean Water Act liability, which critics of such approaches note could excuse work that does not actually meet water quality standards if done under an approved permit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would end a 19th-century arrangement in which the public's minerals are taken for free while the public pays for abandoned mine cleanup, and the money collected would go to a dedicated reclamation fund rather than general revenue. The main cost is higher compliance expense for the mining industry and slower permitting, which could affect jobs in mining-dependent communities, though the bill exempts small producers and grandfathers existing operations at a lower royalty rate. On balance the gains to taxpayers and communities outweigh the industry costs, though the permitting layer is genuinely heavier than what exists today.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, neither ever reported it out, and the session ended with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Hardrock Mining and Reclamation Act of 2014 on July 10, 2014, and it was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
Within days it was sent to subcommittees—Energy and Mineral Resources under Natural Resources and Water Resources and Environment under Transportation—on July 11 and July 18, 2014.
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill had 25 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, mining on federal land continued with no royalty, no claim maintenance fee increase, no full-cost cleanup bonding, and no dedicated fund to reclaim abandoned mines, leaving cleanup costs on taxpayers. Communities with contaminated abandoned mines got no new cleanup money either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; with no roll-call ever taken, the record shows the bill had support only from one party and never moved under the other party's control.

industries.note: The bill would charge an 8% royalty for the first time, plus claim fees and a per-ton reclamation fee, and require full-cost cleanup bonds; under current law these minerals come off federal land with no royalty and cleanup costs often fall to taxpayers. The industry's interest in the bill ran against the public's interest in being compensated and protected.

Producers with under $100,000 in annual mineral income and claimants holding 10 or fewer claims are exempted from the royalty, reclamation fee, and maintenance fee, so small family-scale operations keep operating essentially as before.
The mandatory financial assurance requirement would create demand for bonds and other financial instruments covering mine cleanup; this cost exists because it shifts cleanup risk away from taxpayers.
